answers.question: How does an O3 frontend module declare its configuration schema so implementers can override its settings? Point to the documentation and implementation.

paragraphs.text: An O3 frontend module declares its settings in a **config schema** — a plain JavaScript/TypeScript object describing every option, its type, its default and its validation. Implementers then override those options in a JSON config file keyed by module name, and the app shell feeds that file into the configuration system, which overlays the implementer's values on top of the schema defaults. Here is the documentation and the code behind it.
## The documentation

The developer-facing guide is **`configuration-system.mdx`** in the `openmrs-contrib-o3-docs` repo — "The Configuration System" [1]. It explains the schema keywords (`_type`, `_default`, `_description`, `_validators`, `_elements`), how to write validators, arrays and nested objects, and how to read the values back [2]. The page says explicitly that its audience is module developers, and points implementers elsewhere [3].

The implementer-facing guide is **`configure-o3/overview.mdx`** — "Configure O3" [4]. It shows the config-file format: each key is a module name and the value holds the properties to override, with a worked example for `@openmrs/esm-patient-chart-app` and `@openmrs/esm-primary-navigation-app` [5]. Task-specific pages sit under `content/en-US/docs/configure-o3/`, e.g. `configure-the-patient-chart.mdx` and `configure-branding.mdx`.
## What a module writes

A module keeps its schema in a `config-schema.ts` and exports it as an object. `esm-patient-chart-app` is a good example: `esmPatientChartSchema` lists options such as `encounterEditableDuration` (a number with default 0), `notesConceptUuids` (an array whose `_elements` are concept UUIDs) and a nested `logo` group [6].
The module registers that schema in its `startupApp()` entry point with `defineConfigSchema`, before any component renders [7]. The docs describe this same pattern for Core v5+ modules [8].

Schema keywords are the values prefixed with `_`: `_type` (from the `Type` enum), `_default`, `_description`, `_validators` and `_elements` for arrays or object maps. The `Type` enum covers `String`, `Number`, `Boolean`, `Array`, `Object`, `UUID`, `ConceptUuid`, `PersonAttributeTypeUuid` and `PatientIdentifierTypeUuid` [9]. The docs list the same set and warn that all config is optional, so every element needs a default [10].
## What the framework does with it — `esm-core`
Everything lives in the framework package `@openmrs/esm-config` inside `esm-core`, whose public surface is exported from `public.ts` [11] and re-exported through `@openmrs/esm-framework`.

`defineConfigSchema(moduleName, schema)` first runs `validateConfigSchema` to catch developer mistakes, then merges the module's schema with the **implicit schema** every module gets, and stores the result under the module name [12]. The implicit schema holds the two reserved keys, `Display conditions` (privileges and expression for extension visibility) and `Translation overrides` [13], matching the "Automatic schema features" section of the docs [14]. Because these are reserved, `validateConfigSchema` logs an error if a module declares either name itself [15].

Extensions can have their own schema via `defineExtensionConfigSchema`, registered under the extension name from `routes.json` rather than the module name [16]. The docs cover this in the "Extension-specific configuration" section [17].
## How an implementer's override reaches the module

1. The implementer writes a JSON file keyed by module name and points the SPA at it through `configUrls` in `spa-build-config.json` [18].
2. At runtime the app shell fetches those files and calls `provide(config.value, config.name)` for each one [19]; `provide` appends them to the internal store's `providedConfigs` [20].
3. Any change to an input store triggers `recomputeAllConfigs`, which recomputes each module's config [21].
4. For each module, `getConfigForModule` merges the provided configs (including the Implementer Tools temporary config), validates the structure, then `setDefaults` fills any key the implementer left out from the schema's `_default` values, and the validators run over the finished tree [22].

The precedence chain the docs describe — schema defaults, then config files in load order, then Implementer Tools temporary config [23] — is exactly this order: `getProvidedConfigs` returns provided configs followed by the temporary config [24], and arrays are replaced wholesale rather than merged by index [25].

A module then reads the resolved values either with the async `getConfig(moduleName)`, which strips the reserved keys before resolving [26], or in React with the `useConfig` hook, which picks the module up from the component's `moduleName` context [27].

```mermaid
---
title: "Config schema to implementer override"
---
sequenceDiagram
  participant Dev as Module developer
  participant Core as esm-config
  participant Impl as Implementer
  participant Shell as App shell
  Dev->>Core: defineConfigSchema(moduleName, schema)
  Core->>Core: validate, merge implicit schema
  Impl->>Shell: config.json in configUrls
  Shell->>Core: provide(config, name)
  Core->>Core: merge provided and temporary config
  Core->>Core: setDefaults fills schema _defaults
  Core->>Core: run validators
  Dev->>Core: getConfig or useConfig
  Core-->>Dev: resolved config values
```
## Points to note

- Validators only warn: a failed validation logs to the console and the application keeps running with the value [28].
- The implementer's config file needs no entry for options it does not change; defaults fill in [29].
- The backend's Initializer module also accepts frontend config at `configuration/frontend_configuration/config.json`, but per the docs those files must currently be extracted and added to `configUrls` manually [30].

I read only the English docs (`content/en-US`); parallel French copies exist and I did not check whether they match. I also did not inspect every module's schema — the pattern above is verified in `openmrs-esm-patient-chart` and the framework, and the same `defineConfigSchema` call appears in many other module entry points.

It enables developers to define schemas that specify what configuration options are available, their types, defaults, and validation rules.

**For implementers**: If you're looking to configure an existing O3 instance (changing logos, translations, module settings, etc.), see the [Configure O3](/docs/configure-o3/overview) guide instead. This guide is for **developers** who want to make their modules configurable.
A framework is provided to make configurability easier for developers and configuring easier for implementers.

**For implementers**: To learn how to configure your O3 instance, see the [Configure O3](/docs/configure-o3/overview) guide, which covers practical configuration tasks like branding, translations, and module-specific settings.
### How to make a frontend module configurable
You should use the OpenMRS Frontend Framework to make modules configurable.
The main task is to create a config schema for your module. The config schema is what tells the framework what configuration files should look like, including defaults and validations.

**Note**: Configuration schemas are optional. If your module doesn't need any configuration options (for example, if it's a library module like the [React Form Engine](https://github.com/openmrs/openmrs-esm-form-engine-lib) that receives all its configuration through props or function parameters), you don't need to define a schema. The configuration system will still work; modules without schemas use the implicit schema for `Display conditions` and `Translation overrides`.

You’ll probably start with some idea of what you want configs for your module to look like. Try and put yourself in the implementer’s shoes and imagine what features they will expect to be configurable, and what they might expect the configuration property to be called. Assume they don’t know anything about the internal workings of your module.
In the following section, we’ll see how to write a config schema that supports these config elements.

We’ll start with just that first nested config element from above, `hologram.color`. We must provide defaults for all of the values—in OpenMRS Frontend 3.0, all configuration is optional. All modules should do something reasonable out of the box.

- `Translation overrides` - Used for per-language translation overrides

Typically, you'll need to make multiple configuration overrides to various frontend modules. The standard approach is to create a JSON configuration file that is accessible via HTTP/HTTPS on your server. You can then point your SPA to this configuration file by specifying its URL in the `configUrls` array of the SPA build configuration file (`spa-build-config.json`). Alternatively, you can include frontend configuration in content packages (see "Content package frontend configuration" below).

If it returns `false`, validation fails and the second argument to `validator` is used as the error message. You can also provide a custom validator function directly in `_validators`; direct validators should return `undefined` for success or an error string for failure.

**Important**: When validation fails, the error is logged to the browser console, but the application continues to run. Invalid configuration values are still used—validation errors serve as warnings to help implementers identify and fix configuration problems, rather than preventing the application from starting.

Configuration files specified in `configUrls` are fetched at runtime (when the SPA loads), not during the build process. The app shell fetches them together, then provides them to the configuration system in the order specified in the array. When merging configurations, later files override earlier ones, so the last file in the array has the highest precedence among config files. Content packages can include frontend configuration files at `configuration/frontend_configuration/config.json`. These files provide distro-level configuration overrides. Currently, these files need to be manually extracted from content packages and made accessible via HTTP/HTTPS (either by serving them from your web server or adding their URLs to `configUrls`). In the future, the backend may automatically extract and serve these files.

**Note**: The demo content package (`openmrs-content-referenceapplication-demo`) includes a frontend configuration file that configures extension slots. To use it, extract `configuration/frontend_configuration/config.json` from the content package and serve it via HTTP/HTTPS, then add its URL to `configUrls` in `spa-build-config.json`.
